marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q001.takeaway: The cardiogenic area arises in splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm, where paired endothelial heart tubes develop before fusing into the primitive heart tube.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q001.displayText: The cardiogenic area forms within the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm, also called splanchnopleuric mesoderm. Angioblastic tissue in this region gives rise to paired endothelial heart tubes. The cardiac progenitor field initially lies cranial to the neural folds as a horseshoe-shaped area; subsequent embryonic folding changes its position as the heart tubes approach and fuse. Thus, for the embryologic origin of the cardiogenic area and primitive heart tubes, the key mesodermal compartment is splanchnopleuric mesoderm.
emphasis: splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm

rationales.a: Extraembryonic mesoderm contributes extraembryonic vascular and supporting tissues, but the embryonic cardiogenic area is derived from intraembryonic splanchnic lateral plate mesoderm.
rationales.b: Somatopleuric mesoderm is the somatic layer associated with body-wall structures; it is not the layer that forms the cardiogenic heart tubes.
rationales.d: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites and their derivatives rather than the cardiogenic field.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q003.takeaway: The proximal one-third of bulbus cordis forms the trabeculated right ventricle; primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated left ventricle.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q003.displayText: The trabeculated part of the right ventricle develops from the proximal one-third of the bulbus cordis. During cardiac looping, the primitive heart tube is reorganized into recognizable inflow, ventricular, and outflow regions. The middle third of bulbus cordis, the conus cordis, contributes the ventricular outflow tracts, while the distal third, the truncus arteriosus, contributes the roots and proximal portions of the great arteries. In contrast, the primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated part of the left ventricle. This right-versus-left ventricular derivative distinction is the key discriminator.
emphasis: proximal one-third of the bulbus cordis
primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated part of the left ventricle

rationales.a: Primitive ventricle forms the trabeculated left ventricle, not the trabeculated right ventricle.
rationales.b: The distal third of bulbus cordis corresponds to truncus arteriosus and contributes proximal great-artery structures rather than trabeculated right ventricle.
rationales.c: The middle third, or conus cordis, contributes the smooth ventricular outflow tracts rather than the trabeculated right ventricle.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q004.takeaway: Each sinus venosus horn receives vitelline, umbilical, and common cardinal veins; subcardinal veins instead develop with the urogenital venous system.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q004.displayText: The sinus venosus is the caudal inflow portion of the primitive heart and has right and left horns. Each horn receives three paired venous systems: vitelline veins from the yolk-sac region, umbilical veins carrying placental blood, and common cardinal veins draining the embryonic body wall. Subcardinal veins are not direct tributaries of the sinus venosus; they arise later in association with the urogenital ridges and contribute importantly to renal and inferior vena caval development. Therefore subcardinal vein is the exception.
emphasis: Subcardinal veins are not direct tributaries of the sinus venosus

rationales.a: Vitelline veins are normal tributaries of the sinus venosus and carry blood from the yolk-sac region.
rationales.b: Umbilical veins are normal sinus-venosus tributaries carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta.
rationales.c: Common cardinal veins are normal sinus-venosus tributaries that drain the embryonic body wall.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q005.takeaway: The left horn of sinus venosus becomes the coronary sinus, whereas the right horn is incorporated into the smooth part of the right atrium.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q005.displayText: The coronary sinus develops from the left horn of the sinus venosus, so failure of this structure can produce congenital absence or abnormality of the coronary sinus. As venous return shifts toward the right, the right horn enlarges and becomes incorporated into the right atrium, while the left horn regresses and persists principally as the coronary sinus. Nearby venous derivatives should be kept separate: the right common cardinal vein contributes to the superior vena cava, the right vitelline pathway contributes to the terminal inferior vena cava, and the left common cardinal vein contributes to the oblique vein of the left atrium.
emphasis: left horn of the sinus venosus
right horn enlarges and becomes incorporated into the right atrium
left common cardinal vein contributes to the oblique vein of the left atrium

rationales.a: The right umbilical vein normally obliterates and is not the embryologic source of the coronary sinus.
rationales.b: The right horn of sinus venosus is incorporated mainly into the smooth-walled part of the right atrium rather than forming the coronary sinus.
rationales.d: The left vitelline vein is not the source of the coronary sinus; the relevant persistent sinus-venosus derivative is the left horn.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q006.takeaway: Persistent left superior vena cava most commonly results from failure of regression of the left anterior cardinal vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q006.displayText: A persistent left-sided superior vena cava results from persistence of the left anterior cardinal venous channel that normally regresses during remodeling of the cardinal system. It commonly drains through the coronary sinus and may be discovered incidentally. Normal superior vena cava formation instead depends on the proximal right anterior cardinal vein together with the right common cardinal vein. The transverse anastomosis between anterior cardinal veins contributes to the left brachiocephalic vein. Thus the key developmental error in a persistent left SVC is failure of regression of the left anterior cardinal vein.
emphasis: failure of regression of the left anterior cardinal vein
proximal right anterior cardinal vein together with the right common cardinal vein

rationales.b: The right anterior cardinal system is retained in normal SVC formation; its regression would not explain a persistent left SVC.
rationales.c: The left common cardinal vein contributes to left-sided venous remnants such as the oblique vein/coronary-sinus region, but persistent left SVC classically reflects persistence of the left anterior cardinal vein.
rationales.d: The right posterior cardinal vein participates in caudal venous development and is not the channel whose persistence creates a left-sided SVC.

marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q007.takeaway: The post-renal segment of the inferior vena cava is derived mainly from the right supracardinal vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH06_Q007.displayText: The inferior vena cava is a composite vessel assembled from several embryonic venous channels. Its post-renal, or supracardinal, segment develops mainly from the right supracardinal vein. More cranially, the pre-renal segment is chiefly subcardinal in origin, the renal segment forms through the subcardinal–supracardinal anastomosis, and the hepatic termination is related to the right vitelline/hepatocardiac channel. Keeping these segmental origins separate makes the post-renal question straightforward: right supracardinal vein is the principal source.
emphasis: pre-renal segment is chiefly subcardinal in origin

rationales.b: The umbilical vein carries placental blood and does not form the post-renal IVC segment.
rationales.c: Anterior cardinal veins primarily contribute to venous drainage of the upper body and SVC/brachiocephalic system, not the post-renal IVC.
rationales.d: The right hepatocardiac channel contributes to the hepatic/terminal IVC region, not the post-renal segment.
